EU rules on carbon dioxide emissions from new cars and vans do not set a limit for each vehicle. Instead, they set targets for the average emissions of all the new vehicles that a manufacturer registers in the EU in a given year. A manufacturer's individual target depends partly on the average mass of its fleet, so a producer of heavier cars is allowed somewhat higher average emissions than one selling mainly small models. Manufacturers may also form pools and be assessed together, which lets a company with few zero-emission models combine its figures with one that sells many.

A manufacturer whose average exceeds its target pays an excess emissions premium of €95 for each gram per kilometre above the target, multiplied by the number of new vehicles it registered that year. Because the premium applies across the whole fleet, even a small excess can become expensive for a large producer.

The 2023 revision of the rules tightened the targets for 2030 to a 55% cut for cars and a 50% cut for vans, compared with 2021 levels. In 2025, after carmakers warned that they faced heavy penalties, the EU allowed manufacturers to show compliance with their 2025 targets on the basis of their average performance over 2025, 2026 and 2027, rather than for 2025 alone. Critics argued that the change rewarded firms that had been slow to invest.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A manufacturer's emission target is determined by the average mass of the new cars and vans that it registers in the EU in a given year.
Every new car registered in the EU must individually stay below the emission target that applies to the manufacturer that sells it.
A carmaker over its 2025 target owes no premium for that year if better results in 2026 and 2027 bring its three-year average into line.
The flexibility for 2025 was introduced mainly because sales of electric cars had fallen sharply across most of the EU in the preceding year.

Revised EU rules on the rights of rail passengers have applied since June 2023. When a train arrives at the final destination 60 to 119 minutes late, passengers are entitled to compensation of 25% of the ticket price; for a delay of two hours or more, the figure rises to 50%. Railway undertakings may set a minimum threshold, of no more than €4, below which compensation is not paid. Passengers who were already informed of a delay before they bought their ticket have no right to compensation for it.

The revision added a new exception. A carrier no longer owes compensation if the delay is caused by extraordinary circumstances such as extreme weather, a major natural disaster or a major public health crisis, provided that it could not have been avoided. Strikes by the carrier's own staff, however, do not count as extraordinary circumstances. The exception concerns compensation only: it does not remove the carrier's duties to inform and assist passengers and to offer them rerouting.

If the carrier does not communicate rerouting options within 100 minutes of the scheduled departure time, passengers may arrange alternative public transport themselves and claim back the necessary, appropriate and reasonable costs. Member States may exempt urban, suburban and regional services from parts of the regulation.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Someone who bought an €80 ticket before a strike by the carrier's own staff was announced, and arrives 90 minutes late as a result, is owed €20.
Once a delay is caused by extreme weather that could not have been avoided, the carrier no longer owes its passengers either assistance or an offer of rerouting.
The 2023 revision was mainly intended to bring the rights of rail passengers into line with those already enjoyed by air passengers.
Member States may exempt any rail service, including long-distance international trains, from the whole of the regulation.

passage:
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) is designed to put a fair price on the carbon emitted during the production of certain goods entering the EU. It addresses 'carbon leakage': the risk that production moves to countries with weaker climate policies, or that EU products are replaced by more carbon-intensive imports, which would shift emissions abroad rather than reduce them. The mechanism covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen.

During a transitional phase from October 2023 to the end of 2025, importers only had to report the emissions embedded in their goods; no payment was due. The definitive regime began in January 2026. Importers must now be authorised and will surrender CBAM certificates whose price follows that of allowances in the EU Emissions Trading System. If a carbon price has already been paid in the country of production, it can be deducted from the amount owed. A simplification adopted in 2025 exempted importers bringing in less than 50 tonnes of covered goods a year, which removed most importers from the scheme while keeping the vast majority of embedded emissions within it.

At the same time, the free emission allowances that EU producers in the same sectors have received are being phased out gradually between 2026 and 2034, so that domestic and imported goods face a comparable carbon cost.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The mechanism ensures that imported and EU-made goods always bear exactly the same carbon cost, whatever the sector.
Since the 2025 simplification, the mechanism no longer applies to most of the emissions embedded in imports of covered goods.
Revenue from the sale of CBAM certificates is to be paid mainly into the EU budget rather than kept by the Member States.
A cement importer can deduct a carbon price already paid where the cement was made from what it owes under CBAM.

Emissions from road transport, the heating of buildings, agriculture, waste and small industrial installations are not covered by the EU Emissions Trading System for power and heavy industry. They fall instead under the Effort Sharing Regulation, whose sectors together account for around 60% of the EU's domestic greenhouse gas emissions. Since its revision in 2023, the regulation requires these emissions to fall by 40% across the EU by 2030 compared with 2005.

The EU-wide target is divided into binding national targets ranging from a 10% to a 50% reduction. They were set mainly on the basis of gross domestic product per person, so that wealthier Member States carry a larger share of the effort, with some adjustment to reflect where cuts can be made cost-effectively. Each country receives a declining annual emission allocation for every year up to 2030.

Member States have several flexibilities. They can bank surplus allocations for later years, borrow a limited amount from the following year, and buy or sell allocations among themselves. Some may also use a limited quantity of removals from land use and forestry, and a few were allowed to cancel a set number of emissions trading allowances to count towards their targets. Environmental groups have warned that generous use of these options could allow some countries to postpone domestic cuts.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Every Member State must reduce its emissions in the effort-sharing sectors by 40% by 2030 compared with 2005.
A Member State with a high income per head will normally have been set a steeper reduction target than a poorer one.
Environmental groups have shown that the flexibilities allow several countries to postpone cuts in their domestic emissions.
Wealthier Member States carry the entire burden of cutting emissions in the sectors covered by the Effort Sharing Regulation.

passage:
The Renewable Energy Directive sets the EU's overall target for the share of energy that comes from renewable sources. Its 2023 revision raised the binding target for 2030 to at least 42.5% of gross final energy consumption, almost double the share recorded in 2020, and added an indicative top-up of 2.5 percentage points that would bring the total to 45%. The target is binding on the EU as a whole rather than on each Member State: countries set out their own contributions in national energy and climate plans, and the Commission can recommend more ambitious efforts if the sum falls short.

Because slow permitting had become a major obstacle, the revision also requires Member States to designate 'renewables acceleration areas' where projects are expected to have limited environmental impact. Inside these areas, the permit procedure for a new installation should in principle not exceed twelve months, against two years outside them, and longer periods apply to offshore projects. Renewable energy plants are also presumed to be in the overriding public interest, which makes it easier for them to benefit from exemptions under certain environmental rules.

Some environmental organisations have welcomed faster permitting but cautioned that acceleration areas must be mapped carefully to avoid harm to sensitive habitats.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Inside renewables acceleration areas, every permit procedure for a new installation is completed within twelve months.
The 42.5% target is binding only on the EU as a whole, not on each Member State individually.
The Commission has recommended more ambitious efforts to several Member States whose contributions fell short.
Acceleration areas are likely to be located mainly on land that has already been built on or degraded by industry.

The Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, which entered into force in July 2024, extends the EU's ecodesign approach from energy-related products to almost all physical goods placed on the EU market. Food, feed, medicinal products and motor vehicles are among the exclusions. The regulation does not itself set requirements for particular products. Instead, it provides a framework under which the Commission adopts detailed rules, product group by product group, on aspects such as durability, reparability, recycled content and substances that hinder recycling. The first working plan, published in 2025, gave priority to textiles, furniture, mattresses, tyres, iron and steel, and aluminium, among others.

Products covered by such rules will have to carry a digital product passport, giving customers, repairers and authorities access to information about their composition and environmental performance.

The regulation also contains rules that apply without further acts. From July 2026, large companies may no longer destroy unsold clothing, clothing accessories and footwear. Medium-sized companies will be bound from 2030, while micro and small enterprises are exempt. Large companies must also publish each year how many unsold consumer products they discarded and why. Supporters say the ban removes an incentive to overproduce; some retailers argue that donation and resale channels cannot absorb all surplus stock.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Each product sold on the EU market will have to carry a digital product passport under the regulation.
Textiles were made a priority because the sector generates more waste than any other product group in the EU.
Since July 2026, large companies have been banned from destroying all of their unsold consumer products.
In 2027, a medium-sized clothing firm can still destroy unsold garments without breaching this regulation.

The EU Batteries Regulation, adopted in 2023, replaced a directive from 2006 and covers batteries throughout their life cycle, from the sourcing of raw materials to collection and recycling. Unlike the directive, it applies directly in all Member States.

Several of its obligations are phased in. From February 2027, portable batteries built into appliances such as phones must in principle be removable and replaceable by the end user, although exemptions exist, for example for devices designed to operate mainly in wet conditions. From the same date, batteries for electric vehicles and for light means of transport such as e-bikes, as well as industrial batteries above 2 kWh, must have a digital battery passport.

The regulation also requires new industrial and electric-vehicle batteries, among others, to contain minimum shares of recycled material. From 2031, these are 16% for cobalt, 85% for lead, 6% for lithium and 6% for nickel; the shares for cobalt, lithium and nickel rise in 2036, while the lead share stays the same. Collection targets for waste portable batteries rise from 45% in 2023 to 63% by the end of 2027 and 73% by the end of 2030.

Recyclers argue that the recycled-content rules will create a stable market for recovered metals, but some manufacturers doubt that enough material will be available in time.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Between 2023 and 2030, the collection target for waste portable batteries rises by 28 percentage points.
All phones sold in the EU from February 2027 must have batteries that their owners can remove and replace.
The recycled-content rules are expected to reduce the EU's dependence on imported cobalt and lithium.
Battery manufacturers agree that there will not be enough recycled material to meet the 2031 shares.

The EU Deforestation Regulation, adopted in 2023, targets seven commodities: cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya and wood, together with many products made from them, such as chocolate, leather, furniture and printed paper. Such goods may be placed on the EU market or exported from it only if they are deforestation-free, have been produced in accordance with the laws of the country of production, and are covered by a due diligence statement.

'Deforestation-free' means that the commodities were not produced on land deforested after 31 December 2020; for wood, the forest must also not have been degraded after that date. To prove this, operators must collect the geographical coordinates of the plots where the commodities were produced. The rules apply equally to goods produced inside and outside the EU.

The Commission classifies countries, or parts of them, as presenting low, standard or high risk. The classification affects the intensity of checks: national authorities must check at least 1% of operators sourcing from low-risk countries, 3% for standard risk and 9% for high risk. Operators sourcing from low-risk countries benefit from simplified due diligence, although they still have to collect information.

The application of the regulation has been postponed, after businesses and several trading partners said they needed more time to prepare.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Most of the deforestation linked to consumption in the EU is caused by the production of soya and palm oil.
Because the regulation is aimed at imports, wood harvested in the forests of EU Member States falls outside the scope of its rules.
Soya grown on a field cleared of forest in 2019 meets the regulation's condition of being deforestation-free.
Any product that contains wood, rubber or cocoa falls within the scope of the regulation's requirements.

The EU's revised Ambient Air Quality Directive, which entered into force in December 2024, sets stricter limit values to be met by 2030. The annual limit for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) falls from 25 to 10 micrograms per cubic metre, and that for nitrogen dioxide from 40 to 20. These values move the EU closer to the guidelines published by the World Health Organization in 2021, which are lower still at 5 and 10 micrograms respectively, and the directive provides for regular reviews of whether further alignment is appropriate.

Member States may ask to postpone the 2030 deadline, to 2040 at the latest, if they can show with modelling that the limits cannot be met in time despite appropriate measures, for example because of specific geographic or climatic conditions. Any postponement depends on an air quality roadmap.

The directive also strengthens citizens' rights. People whose health has been damaged by a breach of the rules are entitled to claim compensation, and members of the public must have access to justice to challenge decisions on the directive's implementation. Some industry groups have argued that the new limits will be costly to meet in regions with heavy traffic or industry, while health organisations wanted full alignment with the WHO values from the outset.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The limits were tightened after studies linked air pollution to many thousands of early deaths in the EU.
Any Member State may decide to delay meeting the new limit values until 2040 if it finds them too costly.
Most cities in the EU already comply with the limit for fine particulate matter that applies from 2030.
The new EU annual limit for nitrogen dioxide is double the value recommended by the WHO.

Adopted in 1991, the Nitrates Directive aims to protect waters from pollution caused by nitrates from agricultural sources, mainly fertilisers and livestock manure. Excess nitrogen that is not taken up by crops can leach into groundwater or run off into rivers and coastal waters, where it contributes to eutrophication: the excessive growth of algae, which can deplete oxygen and harm aquatic life.

Member States must identify waters that are, or could become, polluted, using among other criteria a threshold of 50 milligrams of nitrate per litre in groundwater and in surface water used for drinking. The land draining into these waters is designated as nitrate vulnerable zones, although a country may choose instead to apply the measures across its whole territory. In vulnerable zones, farmers must follow action programmes that include periods when spreading fertiliser is prohibited, rules on storing manure and a limit on the quantity of nitrogen from livestock manure that can be applied: 170 kilograms per hectare per year.

The Commission may grant derogations allowing higher amounts in specific conditions, for instance on farms with a long growing season and crops that take up a lot of nitrogen, such as grassland. Member States must report on water quality every four years, and the Commission has repeatedly taken countries to court over insufficient designation or weak action programmes.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Farmers in vulnerable zones can never spread more than 170 kg of manure nitrogen per hectare in a year.
A Member State may apply action programmes throughout its territory rather than designating particular zones.
Nitrate pollution from agriculture in the EU has fallen steadily since the directive was adopted in 1991.
The 50 mg/l threshold was chosen because higher nitrate levels in drinking water are dangerous for infants.

The Nature Restoration Regulation, in force since August 2024, sets binding targets for restoring damaged ecosystems, going beyond earlier EU laws that focused on protecting those that remain. Its adoption was close: after months of opposition from some farming organisations and political groups, it passed in the Council only when one minister voted in favour against the wishes of her own country's head of government.

Overall, the EU must put in place restoration measures covering at least 20% of its land and 20% of its sea areas by 2030, and measures for all ecosystems in need of restoration by 2050. For habitat types listed in the regulation, Member States must restore at least 30% of the area in poor condition by 2030, 60% by 2040 and 90% by 2050. Other targets concern urban green space, the reconnection of rivers, with the aim of restoring at least 25,000 kilometres to a free-flowing state, and the planting of at least three billion additional trees across the EU by 2030.

Each Member State has to prepare a national restoration plan setting out how it will meet the targets. The regulation also contains an 'emergency brake' allowing targets for agricultural ecosystems to be suspended temporarily if exceptional events seriously reduce the land available for food production.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: The regulation got through the Council thanks to a minister who voted for it against her head of government's wishes.
The regulation contains no restoration targets for urban areas or rivers, which are left to the Member States.
All of the regulation's targets can be suspended for a time if exceptional events threaten food production.
National restoration plans had to be submitted to the European Commission by September 2026 at the latest.

Before 2022, the EU had no common rules on how full underground gas storage had to be before winter. That changed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, when supply cuts and price spikes exposed the risk of entering the cold months with low stocks. A regulation adopted in June 2022 required Member States with storage facilities to have them filled to at least 80% by 1 November 2022 and to at least 90% by 1 November in later years.

The obligation was adapted to national circumstances. Countries with large storage capacity relative to their consumption did not have to fill beyond a volume equal to 35% of their average annual gas consumption over the previous five years. Member States without storage facilities on their territory had to ensure that the equivalent of 15% of their annual consumption was held in storage in other Member States, or contribute to the effort in another agreed way.

The rules were initially due to expire at the end of 2025. In 2025 they were extended until the end of 2027, but with more flexibility over the timing and level of filling, after traders and some governments complained that a rigid deadline pushed up summer prices by signalling to the market exactly when large volumes had to be bought.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Since 2025, Member States have been free to decide for themselves whether to fill their gas storage facilities.
The filling rules were the main reason why European wholesale gas prices fell in the years following 2022.
Under the 2022 rules, not every Member State with storage facilities had to fill them to 90% of their capacity.
The EU met its storage filling target each year from 2022 to 2025, despite the loss of most Russian gas supplies.

passage:
European airspace has traditionally been organised along national borders, with each country responsible for air traffic control over its own territory. As a result, flights often follow routes that are longer than necessary, and controllers in neighbouring centres use systems that are not always compatible. The Single European Sky initiative, which the EU launched with a first legislative package in 2004, aims to manage airspace according to traffic flows rather than borders, in order to improve safety and capacity, cut costs and reduce emissions.

The initiative rests on several instruments. A performance scheme sets targets for air navigation service providers in areas such as delays, cost-efficiency and flight efficiency. A Network Manager, a role entrusted to Eurocontrol, coordinates route design and traffic flows across Europe. SESAR, the technological pillar, develops and deploys new air traffic management systems.

Progress has been slower than its supporters hoped. Member States regard airspace as closely linked to national sovereignty and defence, and military needs restrict how some areas can be used. Functional airspace blocks, intended to merge the management of airspace across borders, largely failed to deliver the expected integration. A reform agreed in 2024 updated the framework, but airlines argue that air traffic control strikes and staff shortages in some countries remain a major cause of delays.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Functional airspace blocks achieved none of the cross-border integration that they were designed to deliver.
Shortening the routes that flights follow is one way in which the initiative is meant to reduce emissions.
SESAR is run as a public-private partnership bringing together the EU, Eurocontrol and the aviation industry.
Airlines blame air traffic control strikes for most of the flight delays recorded in European airspace.

The EU Ecolabel, recognisable by its flower logo, was created in 1992. It is voluntary: companies choose whether to apply for it. Criteria are set for product groups such as cleaning products, paints, textiles and tourist accommodation, and they take account of a product's environmental impact throughout its life cycle, from raw materials to disposal. Applications are assessed by competent bodies in each Member State, and compliance is checked by an independent party rather than simply declared by the producer. Food, drink and medicinal products cannot receive the label.

The Ecolabel competes with hundreds of other environmental labels. Studies for the Commission have found that many green claims on the EU market are vague, misleading or unfounded, and that consumers find it hard to tell credible labels from self-declared ones.

A directive adopted in 2024 to empower consumers for the green transition addresses this problem. From 27 September 2026, traders may no longer make generic environmental claims, such as 'eco-friendly', when they cannot demonstrate recognised excellent environmental performance. Nor may they display sustainability labels that are not based on a certification scheme or established by public authorities. Labels such as the EU Ecolabel are therefore unaffected by this ban, while some retailers' own logos may have to be withdrawn or redesigned.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A producer that meets the criteria may award itself the EU Ecolabel without any outside verification.
Since late 2026, all environmental claims on products are banned unless they are backed by the EU Ecolabel.
Products carrying the EU Ecolabel sell better than comparable products that do not carry the label.
Wine is never eligible for the EU Ecolabel, however sustainably the grapes are grown.

The EU's Waste Framework Directive ranks ways of dealing with waste in a 'waste hierarchy'. Prevention comes first, followed by preparing for re-use, recycling, other recovery such as energy recovery, and finally disposal, for example in landfill. Member States must apply the hierarchy as a priority order, but they may depart from it for specific waste streams where a life-cycle assessment shows that another option gives a better overall environmental outcome.

The directive and related laws contain binding targets for municipal waste, which covers mainly household waste and similar waste from businesses. At least 55% of municipal waste must be prepared for re-use or recycled by 2025, rising to 60% by 2030 and 65% by 2035. By 2035, no more than 10% may be landfilled. In 2023 the Commission warned several Member States that they risked missing the 2025 recycling target.

Separate collection has been extended over time. Since January 2025, Member States have had to collect textiles separately, and a revision of the directive adopted in 2025 requires them to set up extended producer responsibility schemes, under which producers of clothing and footwear pay for the collection and treatment of the textile waste they generate. The same revision sets targets for reducing food waste by 2030, in processing and manufacturing and in retail, restaurants and households.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Landfill is still the most common way of treating municipal waste in the European Union as a whole.
Member States must always follow the waste hierarchy, whatever the waste stream or local conditions.
In the waste hierarchy, the only option ranked below energy recovery is disposal, for example in landfill.
Producer responsibility for textiles was introduced in order to fund the building of new recycling plants.

passage:
Euro emission standards have limited pollutants from new road vehicles in the EU since the early 1990s. The latest, Euro 7, was adopted in 2024. For passenger cars and vans, its limits on exhaust pollutants such as nitrogen oxides are largely the same as under the previous Euro 6 standard. The Commission had proposed stricter values, but these were dropped during negotiations after carmakers and several Member States argued that the cost would divert investment from electric vehicles. For lorries and buses, by contrast, the exhaust limits were tightened.

Euro 7 is nonetheless described by the Commission as the first emission standard worldwide to go beyond the exhaust pipe. It sets limits on particles released by brakes and also covers microplastics from tyre abrasion, which are emitted by all vehicles, including fully electric ones. It also introduces minimum requirements for the durability of batteries in electric and plug-in hybrid cars: a battery must keep at least 80% of its original capacity after five years or 100,000 kilometres, and at least 72% after eight years or 160,000 kilometres.

New car types must comply from November 2026, and all newly registered cars a year later, with later deadlines for heavier vehicles.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Fully electric cars must meet certain Euro 7 requirements even though they have no exhaust pipe.
Euro 7 tightens the exhaust limits for every category of road vehicle compared with Euro 6.
Brake particles are now a larger source of particulate pollution than exhaust from cars.
Carmakers used the savings from unchanged exhaust limits to expand electric car production.

passage:
Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the atmosphere, yet plants cannot use it in its gaseous form. Before the twentieth century, farmers depended on manure, on rotating crops with legumes, whose root bacteria fix nitrogen, and on imported natural deposits such as Chilean saltpetre and guano. By the 1890s, scientists warned that these sources would not be enough to feed a growing world population.

In 1909 the German chemist Fritz Haber demonstrated in the laboratory that ammonia could be synthesised from nitrogen and hydrogen at high temperature and pressure, with the help of a catalyst. Carl Bosch, an engineer at the chemical company BASF, then turned the method into an industrial process, and the first plant began production in 1913. Both men later received Nobel Prizes in Chemistry. During the First World War, which broke out in 1914, the process was also used to supply nitrates for explosives, which helped Germany to continue fighting despite a naval blockade.

Today the Haber–Bosch process supplies most of the nitrogen in synthetic fertilisers. Some researchers estimate that around half of the world's population depends on food grown with it. It is, however, highly energy-intensive, and because the hydrogen is mostly produced from fossil fuels, chiefly natural gas, it is a significant source of carbon dioxide emissions.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Today the process supplies all of the nitrogen used in fertilisers around the world.
Without the process, around half of the world's population would now go hungry.
Haber received his Nobel Prize in Chemistry several years before Bosch received his.
The process was in industrial use before the outbreak of the First World War.

passage:
A solar cell converts light into electricity when photons free electrons in a semiconductor. Each semiconductor has a band gap, the minimum energy a photon must carry to free an electron. Photons with less energy than the band gap pass through without producing current, while photons with more energy produce current but lose the excess as heat. This trade-off sets a ceiling on efficiency.

In 1961 William Shockley and Hans-Joachim Queisser calculated this ceiling for a cell made of a single semiconductor under unconcentrated sunlight. The limit that bears their names is about 33% and is reached with a band gap of around 1.3 to 1.4 electronvolts. Silicon, which dominates the market, has a band gap of about 1.1 electronvolts; its own theoretical maximum, once other unavoidable losses are included, is usually put at around 29%. Good commercial silicon modules now convert more than 20% of sunlight into electricity.

The limit does not apply to cells that stack several materials with different band gaps, each capturing a different part of the solar spectrum. Such tandem cells, for example combining silicon with a perovskite layer, have exceeded 33% in the laboratory, although questions remain about how well perovskites withstand years of outdoor use.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Perovskite layers have been found unable to withstand years of outdoor use in tandem solar cells.
A cell that turns 36% of unconcentrated sunlight into electricity must combine more than one semiconductor.
Silicon dominates the market because it is cheaper to produce than other suitable semiconductors.
Shockley and Queisser predicted in 1961 that stacked cells would one day be able to exceed the limit they had calculated.

Over the past few million years, Earth's climate has swung repeatedly between glacial periods, when ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, and warmer interglacials such as the present one. In the early twentieth century the Serbian engineer Milutin Milanković proposed that these cycles were paced by regular changes in Earth's orbit and axis.

Three changes matter most. The shape of the orbit varies from nearly circular to slightly elliptical over a cycle of roughly 100,000 years. The tilt of Earth's axis varies between about 22.1 and 24.5 degrees over around 41,000 years; a greater tilt makes summers warmer and winters colder in both hemispheres. Finally, the axis slowly wobbles, or precesses, which shifts the season in which Earth is closest to the Sun over a cycle of roughly 23,000 years. These changes alter the total sunlight Earth receives over a year very little, but they redistribute it between seasons and latitudes. What appears to matter most is summer sunshine at high northern latitudes, which decides whether winter snow survives to build ice sheets.

Milanković's theory gained wide acceptance after 1976, when analysis of deep-sea sediment cores revealed climate cycles matching his periods. Scientists stress, however, that orbital changes act as a pacemaker: feedbacks involving carbon dioxide and the reflectivity of ice amplify their effect.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A smaller axial tilt tends to cool far-northern summers, which in turn helps winter snow to persist there.
Changes in Earth's orbit and axis are enough on their own to explain the full scale of glacial cycles.
The present interglacial is expected to continue for tens of thousands of years, whatever humans do.
Scientists have established that northern summer sunshine is what determines the growth of ice sheets.

passage:
Grey wolves were eliminated from Yellowstone National Park in the United States by the 1920s, mainly through government predator-control programmes. In 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves captured in Canada were released in the park, and the population grew quickly. The reintroduction has since become one of the most cited examples of a trophic cascade, in which a top predator affects plants and landscapes indirectly through its effect on the animals it eats.

In the popular version of the story, wolves reduced the number of elk and also made them avoid risky places such as river banks. Willows and aspens, previously browsed heavily by elk, recovered; beavers returned; and stream banks stabilised. This 'landscape of fear' explanation spread widely through documentaries and online videos.

Many ecologists consider this account too simple. Elk numbers were also reduced by human hunting outside the park, by drought and by other predators such as bears and cougars, whose numbers rose during the same period. Some field studies tracking individual elk found little evidence that they avoided areas where wolves were most active. Some researchers argue that willows in places once heavily browsed have failed to recover because, with beavers long absent, streams have cut deeper channels and water tables have fallen. Most scientists agree that wolves have affected the park's ecosystem, but the strength of the effect remains disputed.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone in order to reduce the size of the elk herds that lived in the park.
Field studies have shown that elk never avoid the parts of the park where wolves are most active.
A fall in Yellowstone's elk population after 1995 would not by itself show that wolves were the cause.
Field studies have disproved the popular account of how wolves changed the park's landscape.

In the 1880s, two systems competed to supply electricity in the United States. Thomas Edison's companies promoted direct current (DC), which flows in one direction, while George Westinghouse, using patents licensed from Nikola Tesla, backed alternating current (AC), which reverses direction many times a second. The rivalry, later called the 'war of the currents', included public campaigns in which Edison's side stressed the dangers of high-voltage AC.

AC won mainly because of the transformer, which could raise its voltage for transmission and lower it again for safe use in homes. Transmitting power at high voltage reduces the current needed and therefore the energy lost as heat in the wires. With the technology of the time, DC voltage could not be changed easily, so DC systems needed power stations within a short distance of their customers.

The contest did not end the story of DC. Since the mid-twentieth century, high-voltage direct current (HVDC) links have been built where they perform better than AC, notably over very long distances and for undersea cables, in which AC suffers large losses. The converter stations at each end, which turn AC into DC and back, are expensive, so HVDC is generally chosen only when a link is long enough for its lower line losses to outweigh that cost.
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Edison's campaign about the dangers of AC may have delayed its adoption in some American cities.
HVDC links have now replaced alternating current for long-distance power transmission across the world.
Tesla had worked for one of Edison's companies before his patents were licensed to Westinghouse.
All else being equal, sending power at a higher voltage lowers the energy wasted as heat in the lines.

In 1958 the American scientist Charles David Keeling began measuring the concentration of carbon dioxide in the air at an observatory on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii. The site was chosen because, at an altitude of over 3,000 metres and far from continents, the air there is well mixed and little affected by local sources such as cities or forests. The measurements, which continue today, produced the record now known as the Keeling Curve.

The first readings were around 315 parts per million (ppm). The concentration passed 400 ppm in 2013 and now exceeds 420 ppm, compared with about 280 ppm before the industrial revolution, a value known from air bubbles trapped in ice cores. The rise has not been steady: the annual increase in recent decades has been larger than in the 1960s.

Superimposed on the long-term rise is a seasonal cycle. The concentration falls during the northern growing season, from late spring to early autumn, as plants in the Northern Hemisphere take up carbon dioxide, and rises again in autumn and winter, when decomposition releases it. The Northern Hemisphere dominates the cycle because it contains much more land, and therefore much more vegetation, than the Southern Hemisphere. Measurements at other stations, including one at the South Pole, show a similar long-term rise but a much smaller seasonal swing.
